newsitem.title: USA: Exile flotilla heads to edge of Cuban waters.
newsitem.headline: Exile flotilla heads to edge of Cuban waters.

text.p: A flotilla of boats crewed by Cuban exiles headed toward Cuba on Saturday to promote a national work stoppage on the Communist-ruled Caribbean island, organizers said.
The flotilla was the first of three scheduled for this year, leading up to Pope John Paul's visit to Cuba in early 1998.
Cuba on Thursday described the flotilla as a "new attempt at a provocation" and said it would use "the necessary means" to ensure there were no violations of its territory.
Democracy Movement, the prominent Miami-based Cuban exile group that organized the flotilla, assured U.S. and Cuban authorities it did not intend to enter Cuban waters.

At least three dozen vessels headed to the 12-mile (19-km) limit of Cuban territorial waters in two groups, organizers said. The first departed late on Friday and the second early on Saturday from locations in the Florida Keys.

They were to take up positions off Havana, Caibarien and the eastern tip of Cuba at about 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Saturday for prayer services. The boats were to be joined by a about a dozen aircraft from Miami.
"We had a couple of boats break down, but so far everything seems to be OK," Democracy Movement spokesman Oscar Blanco said early on Saturday.
The U.S. Coast Guard said it was monitoring the flotilla but was not escorting it.

Cuban exiles have organized a number of flotillas to the edge of Cuban territory in the Florida Straits between Florida and Cuba. During one in 1995, a Democracy Movement boat entered Cuban territory and was sideswiped by Cuban military vessels.
In February 1996, Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two unarmed U.S. civilian planes between Florida and Cuba, killing four aviators for the exile group Brothers to the Rescue.

The incident provoked international outrage against Cuba. But President Fidel Castro's government defended its action by saying the planes were violating its territory. Washington said the downed planes were outside Cuban airspace and should not have been shot down.

Democracy Movement said Saturday's flotilla was aimed at publicizing within Cuba the idea of a general strike at an as-yet-undetermined date. The group espouses nonviolent protest with the aim of stirring democratic reforms in Cuba.
Democracy Movement leaders have said they reserve their right as Cuban citizens to enter Cuban territory at any time and intend to exercise that right during the pope's visit.
